authors.name: Binti Jua
authors.bio: Novelist and essayist writing about trade routes, inheritance, and the women who keep families moving. Formerly a newspaper columnist; now publishing directly to readers, one signed chapter at a time. Publishes under a pen name.

authors.name: Kalamu Nyeusi
authors.bio: Economic historian interested in how empires keep their books — and how those books are cooked. Writes slowly, footnotes generously. Publishes under a pen name.

authors.name: Ndoto Usiku
authors.bio: Poet and translator. Two collections in print, a third written entirely on night trains. Believes a poem should cost less than a coffee and last longer. Publishes under a pen name.

authors.name: Mwandishi Huru
authors.bio: Writer and former civic-tech engineer. Essays on institutions, open protocols, and the long argument between convenience and freedom. Publishes under a pen name.

books.title: The Salt Roads
books.subtitle: A novel of caravans and inheritance
books.description: Three generations of women run salt across the Sahel, trading in a currency older than any state that has tried to tax it. When the matriarch dies with her ledgers unfinished, her granddaughter must decide whether the family business is an inheritance or a debt. A sweeping, intimate novel about what we carry and who we carry it for.

chapters.title: The Weight of White
content: The salt came out of the earth in slabs the colour of old teeth, and Hadiza had been taught to judge it the way other girls were taught to judge cloth: by weight, by grain, by the faint sound it made when a fingernail was drawn across its face. Good salt sang. Bad salt was quiet, and quiet things, her grandmother said, were always hiding water.

They left Bilma before the sun had decided what kind of day it would be. Forty camels, eleven drivers, and a radio that only caught the BBC between the hours of four and five. Hadiza walked at the back with the ledger pressed flat against her ribs, because the ledger was the only thing in the caravan that could not be replaced.

Her grandmother had kept accounts in three scripts and two languages, and in the margins, in a fourth hand that Hadiza did not recognise, someone had written prices that made no sense — numbers too small for salt, too large for kindness. She read them every night by torchlight and every morning they meant something different.

At the well at Fachi the men spoke of a new man at the checkpoint, young and polite, who asked for papers no one had ever been asked for and wrote everything down in a notebook with a blue cover. "He is building a record," said Musa, spitting into the sand. "And a record is just a debt that has not been sent yet."

That night the wind turned and the desert went silver under a moon that seemed too close. Hadiza opened the ledger to the last page her grandmother had touched and found, beneath a smear of indigo, a single line addressed to her by name. It was not a price. It was a route.

books.title: Letters from the Harmattan
books.subtitle: Essays on dust, distance, and home
books.description: A collection of epistolary essays written during the dry season, when the harmattan wind carries the Sahara south and turns Lagos the colour of a photograph left in the sun. On markets, mothers, migration, and the strange intimacy of a city that is always arriving.

chapters.title: Dear Dust
content: Dear dust — you arrive every December without invitation and every December we pretend to be surprised. You settle on the windscreens and the white shirts and the faces of children, and for three months the whole city looks as though it has been remembered rather than seen.

My mother says the harmattan is the desert visiting its relatives. She says it the way she says everything about the north: with tenderness and a little suspicion, as if the north were a cousin who borrowed money once and never quite mentioned it again.

In Balogun the traders cover their bolts of ankara with plastic and keep selling. Nothing stops for weather here. Weather is a negotiation like any other, and the women who run this market have been negotiating with forces larger than the wind for a very long time.

I keep a list of people who have left. It is not a sad list, exactly; it is more like an address book for a country that exists only in the group chats. Toronto, Houston, Manchester, Dubai. Every name a small border crossed, every border a small sum paid.
This is the letter I did not send: that I stayed not out of courage but out of habit, and that habit, given enough years, begins to look exactly like love.

books.title: Ledger of Kings
books.subtitle: How empires financed themselves — and fell
books.description: From the clipped silver of Rome to the paper promises of the Bourbon kings, a narrative history of sovereign debt told through the account books that survived. A study of what happens when the people who print the money are also the people who keep the score.

chapters.title: The Clipped Denarius
content: In the year 260 a Roman soldier stationed on the Danube was paid in coins that were, by weight, about five percent silver. His grandfather, serving the same empire on the same river, had been paid in coins that were nearly pure. Neither man would have described this as a policy. Both would have recognised it as a lie.

Debasement is the oldest form of taxation that does not require the consent of the taxed. It needs no assembly, no census, no collector at the door. It needs only a mint, a furnace, and a ruler who has decided that the future can be made to pay for the present.

The surviving accounts of the imperial fisc are fragmentary, but what remains is eloquent. The entries grow vaguer as the coinage grows thinner. Where once a clerk recorded the exact weight of silver delivered, he now records only the number of coins — as though, having stopped believing in the metal, the empire had decided to believe in arithmetic instead.

Historians have often treated the monetary collapse of the third century as an economic event. It was, first, an epistemic one. When money stops meaning what it says, every contract becomes a guess and every price a rumour. Trust does not fail all at once; it is drawn down, like a reserve, until one morning it is simply gone.

It is worth remembering that the clerks kept writing. Through the plagues and the usurpers and the barbarian crossings, someone in a cold office sat with a stylus and recorded what the state was owed. The ledger outlived the empire. It usually does.

books.title: The Quiet Republic
books.subtitle: On institutions that work by not being noticed
books.description: Most of what keeps a society free is boring: registries, audits, open meetings, the right to a copy of the record. Mwandishi Huru argues that the quiet machinery of accountability matters more than any election — and shows how it is being dismantled one convenience at a time.

chapters.title: In Praise of Boring Things
content: Nobody has ever marched in defence of a land registry. There are no songs about municipal audit committees, no statues of the clerk who insisted that the minutes be published in full. And yet if you want to know whether a country is free, these are the places to look: not at its anthems, but at its filing cabinets.

A free society is one in which the powerful are obliged to leave a trail. The trail does not need to be glamorous. It needs to be complete, public, and difficult to edit after the fact. Everything else — the speeches, the flags, the ceremonies — is decoration on top of that single, unglamorous obligation.

The threat to this arrangement rarely arrives as a coup. It arrives as an app. A portal that replaces the counter, a platform that replaces the public notice, a terms-of-service agreement that replaces the right of appeal. Each step is easier than the last, and each one moves the record a little further from the people it describes.

I worked for six years building government software, and I can tell you the most dangerous sentence in civic technology: "We can just store it for you." It is always offered as a kindness. It is never only a kindness.

What would it mean to build a republic of receipts — a public life in which every citizen holds a signed copy of every promise made to them? It would mean less convenience and more sovereignty. I think the trade is worth it. This book is my attempt to explain why.

books.title: Protocols of Trust
books.subtitle: Notes toward an internet that can’t be switched off
books.description: A clear-eyed field guide to the protocols — email, BitTorrent, Bitcoin, Nostr — that outlived the companies that tried to own them. Part history, part manifesto, entirely without hype: what open protocols get right, what they get wrong, and why writers in particular should care.

chapters.title: The Protocol Outlives the Platform
content: Email is fifty years old and nobody owns it. That sentence should astonish us more than it does. Every company that has tried to own email — and many have tried — has ended up as merely one more participant in a conversation that existed before it and will continue after it.

The difference between a platform and a protocol is the difference between a building and a language. You can be evicted from a building. You cannot be evicted from a language; you can only stop being understood.

On Nostr, your identity is a key pair. Not an account, not a username leased from a company, but a mathematical fact that you hold. Your public key is how the world recognises you. Your private key is how you prove it is you. Lose the second, and no help desk on earth can give it back — which is precisely the point.

Relays are deliberately dumb. They store signed messages and pass them along, and because every message carries its author’s signature, no relay can forge one. If a relay refuses you, you publish to another. If all of them refuse you, you run your own. The system does not need to trust its servers; it only needs enough of them.

None of this is magic, and anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something. Open protocols are slower, stranger, and less polished than the platforms they replace. Their great virtue is not that they are better. It is that they are yours.

books.title: Small Hours
books.subtitle: Poems written on night trains
books.description: Forty poems composed between midnight and dawn on the sleeper trains of Central Europe. Short, luminous, and occasionally funny, Small Hours is about borders you cross while asleep and the people who share a compartment with you for exactly one night.

chapters.title: Departures
content:
The platform clock
has the patience of a priest.
I have the patience of a woman
with a cold coffee
and a ticket to a city
whose name I cannot pronounce.

Somewhere past Győr
the conductor knocks twice —
once for my passport,
once, I think, for luck.

We are all strangers at this hour,
which is another way of saying
we are all briefly honest.
The man in the top bunk
snores in a language I almost understand.

At the border the train holds its breath.
A dog walks the length of us,
unimpressed by our histories.
Then the long exhale of brakes,
and we are someone else’s country.

Morning arrives the way a rumour does —
first at the edges, then all at once.
I fold the night into my coat pocket
and step out into the light
as if I had always lived here.

books.title: Field Notes on Leaving
books.subtitle: A memoir in small departures
books.description: A translator’s memoir of the twelve times she left somewhere — a country, a language, a marriage, a version of herself — and what each departure taught her about what can and cannot be carried across.

chapters.title: The First Suitcase
content: The first suitcase was my grandmother’s, brown leather gone soft as a glove, with a lock that had not worked since 1956. She gave it to me without ceremony, the way she gave everything — as if the object had simply finished being hers and was ready to become someone else’s.

Translators know a secret that most travellers learn too late: the hardest words to carry are not the long ones. They are the small words, the particles and pronouns, the way one language says "we" and means the family while another says "we" and means the whole nation.

In my first apartment abroad I labelled everything in the kitchen in the new language. Salt, flour, knife, window. For months the labels were a kind of scaffolding, and then one morning I realised I had stopped reading them, and I did not know whether to feel proud or bereaved.

You do not leave a place all at once. You leave it in instalments — a recipe forgotten, an accent softened, a joke you no longer find funny. The bill comes due slowly, and you pay it without noticing, until one day you are fluent in a life you never planned.

What stays is stranger than what goes. A song your mother hummed. The specific grey of a November afternoon. The conviction, irrational and unshakeable, that bread should be bought daily and never on credit.

books.title: Cartographers of Ash
books.subtitle: A novel
books.description: Lisbon, 1755. In the weeks after the great earthquake, a disgraced mapmaker is hired to survey the ruins — and discovers that someone is redrawing the property lines of the dead. A historical thriller about who gets to decide what the map says.

chapters.title: All Saints
content: The earth moved at twenty minutes before ten, while the city was at Mass. João Ferreira was not at Mass. He was in a tavern near the river, drunk on credit, and so he was among the few who saw the sea pull back from the harbour as if gathering its breath.

By the third day the fires had made their own weather. Ash fell on the Rossio like a grey snow, and the survivors moved through it carrying what they could: candlesticks, children, a parrot in a cage, a single shoe. No one carried maps. Maps, it turned out, were the first thing a city forgets.

The Marquis’s secretary found João sleeping in a stable and offered him two things: a pardon for his debts and a commission to survey the ruined Baixa, street by street, house by house. "The king wants to know what was here," the secretary said. "So that he may decide what will be."

He worked with a chain of iron links and a boy named Tiago who could not read but could count to ten thousand without error. Together they walked the lines of houses that no longer existed, and João drew them back into being, one careful rectangle at a time.

It was Tiago who noticed it first: a deed, freshly inked, for a house whose owner they had pulled from the rubble themselves not two weeks before. The signature was confident. The date was a year old. The ink was still wet.
